newsitem.title: USA: U.S. labor cost growth slows in third quarter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. labor cost growth slows in third quarter.

text.p: In a sign that inflationary pressures remain quiet for now, the government reported Tuesday that pay and benefit gains for American workers slowed in the third quarter for the first time in a year.
At the same time, private reports showed a sharp slowdown in the growth of demand for industrial goods in the third quarter and that consumers grew less optimistic in October.
The reports, particularly the wage data, calmed investors' worries about inflation and ignited a rally in financial markets, where stock prices jumped and long-term interest rates fell.

Overall compensation of workers rose 0.6 percent in the third quarter, a smaller rise than had been expected on Wall Street, after a 0.8 percent rise in the second quarter, the Labour Department said.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 58 points to 6,031 and the bellwether 30-year Treasury jumped more than 1-3/4 points, lowering its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price to 6.69 percent from 6.84 percent on Monday.
Investors are hypersensitive that low unemployment could push up wages and prices, and prompt Federal Reserve policy-makers to raise short-term interest rates in a bid to ward off inflation.

The slower rate of growth was the first time since the third quarter of 1995 that compensation gains have moderated and indicated that workers have been unable to capitalise on tightening job markets, reflected by last month's low 5.2 percent unemployment rate.
"The increase was more moderate than one would have expected given the low rate of unemployment," said economist Lynn Reaser of Barnett Banks Inc. in Jacksonville, Fla.
"The overall increase would indicate that there would be less pressure on price increases and less pressure on profit margins than we had seen earlier in the year," she said.
The third quarter increase in the department's Employment Cost Index reflected identical 0.6 percent gains in pay and in the cost of benefits, such as health care.
In the past 12 months, workers' total compensation rose 2.8 percent, little changed from the 2.7 percent gain of the previous 12-month period.
"It suggests that labour costs remain under control despite the fact that you had strong growth," said Sam Kahan, president of ASK Financial Research in Chicago.
Kahan said the threat of job cuts and the reduced inflationary expectations workers have set for themselves may be acting in concert to help keep a lid on wage gains.

The economy, after growing at a brisk 4.7 percent annual rate in the second quarter, is expected to have slowed to 1.8 percent in the third quarter. The Commerce Department will issue its first estimate of third quarter growth on Wednesday.

Separately, the private National Association of Business Economists said its quarterly survey of 104 members found that demand growth weakened across all industries last quarter, with retail and wholesale businesses contracting.
Alhthough less than 3 percent of the economists surveyed think the economy will fall into recession next year, 45 percent expect growth to be sluggish, the association said.
Reflecting that outlook, employers have become more cautious about taking on new workers, it said.

It also said businesses were having trouble making price increases stick, noting more than 75 percent of the firms that tried to raise prices in the third quarter were forced to roll back some or all of their increases.

In another report, the Conference Board said consumer confidence in the economy fell to the weakest level in four months in October. The business research group said its Consumer Confidence Index declined to 106.2 in October from 111.8 in September.

The group said the decline from September was "no cause for alarm," adding that confidence remained relatively strong in most parts of the country. Consumers account for two-thirds of the economy through their purchases of goods and services.

Some economists have said growth in labour costs was being restrained by the temporary slowdown in the increase in benefit costs. Wages and salaries, which represent about 70 percent of the Labour Department's cost index, rose 3.2 percent in the past 12 months, while the cost of benefits rose only 1.8 percent.

Compensation gains for private industry workers in the third quarter slowed to 0.6 percent from 0.8 percent in the second quarter. In the past 12 months, compensation gains rose 2.9 percent after a 2.6 percent rise in the previous 12 months.

For state and local government workers, compensation rose 0.5 percent in the third quarter, down from a 0.7 percent rise in the second quarter. In the past 12 months, state and local government workers' compensation rose 2.5 percent, down from a 3 percent gain in the previous 12 months.
